title: Why Time Speeds Up as You Get Older
desc: Where did the year go? In this calm, sourced deep dive we follow one imagined woman, Hanna, through a quiet New Year's Eve with a box of old diaries, and test seven popular beliefs about time and age against the research: clock time versus felt time, what large surveys really show about age, the old ratio idea, the holiday paradox, memory as a measuring tape, novelty and the oddball effect, the free-fall study on 'slow motion', the body's own clock, emotion and attention, a year in lockdown, the reminiscence bump, and small, gentle ideas that may help a year feel fuller. The last part is a long, gentle wind-down to help you fall asleep.
plan: b01: hook. Hanna (imagined, say so) on New Year's Eve with a box of diaries; 'where did the year go?'; overview list; myth-vs-science framing; clock time vs felt time.

b02: myth 1 (time really speeds up): passage-of-time vs duration in hindsight; waiting room vs day of adventure; myth 2 intro; surveys; Wittmann & Lehnhoff (2005) 499 people 14-94, age at most ~10% of variance.
b03: Friedman & Janssen (2010): students ~21 vs adults ~68, few differences, last ten years only; ~2,000 Dutch 16-80, age 4% / 1%, feeling rushed 10%; ratio idea intro (Janet 1877, James 1890).
b04: myth 3 (just arithmetic): three problems; Hanna's 'nothing much happened' year; myth 4 (time flies when having fun); holiday paradox intro (Hammond 2012).
b05: holiday paradox; Hanna's summer vs blurry year; memory as measuring tape; Avni-Babad & Ritov (2003) routine; well-travelled road; childhood firsts.
b06: fewer firsts, faster years (with caution); novelty: oddball effect (Tse et al. 2004), repetition (Pariyadath & Eagleman 2007).
b07: myth 5 (time slows in a crisis): Stetson, Fiesta & Eagleman (2007) free fall, ~70 mph, 36% longer remembered, could not read fast numbers; memory not slow motion.
b08: Hoagland's wife and the fever count (1930s); Wearden & Penton-Voak (1995); Treisman (1963) pacemaker-counter; Zakay & Block attention gate; myth 6 (one clock).
b09: emotion and attention: Droit-Volet & Meck (2007); boredom, absorption; feelings bend the moment, memories shape the year.
b10: Ogden (2020): 604 UK adults, 7-30 April 2020, >80% felt a change; older and less socially satisfied -> slower; stress, fewer tasks.
b11: reminiscence bump (Rubin, Wetzler & Nebes 1986); myth 7 (nothing can be done); what might help: small firsts, vary the ordinary.
b12: attention, mindfulness (Kramer, Weger & Sharma 2013); keep memories; company; recap of the seven ideas.
b13: Hanna's resolution, closing thought, transition into the wind-down.

b14-b21: wind-down: body scan by the sea, snowy town with bells, a summer lake day, hourglass and a tree through the seasons, a night train, a forest cabin in the rain, a moonlit garden, goodnight and @end teasing 'Why We Put Things Off'.
